newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Cautious Hungary seen avoiding currency trouble.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cautious Hungary seen avoiding currency trouble.

text.p: Hungary, one-time pioneer of economic reform in the former East Bloc, is again poised to become a regional leader as Poland and the Czech Republic struggle to either maintain or restore balance in their economies.

Foreign investors rediscovered Hungary this year following the success of its stabilisation programme launched in 1995 when economic growth virtually stopped and inflation soared. Growth has since returned and is accelerating, macroeconomic stability is greater than ever before and big progress has been made in industrial restructuring.

Direct and near-term capital investment is flowing again. To ensure currency stability, short-term "hot money" is barred from the foreign exchange market and fixed income investment is allowed only in securities with maturity longer than one year.

Currency liberalisation will have to come sooner or later as Hungary races towards membership of the European Union. But for the time being, economists and policymakers agree that recent currency problems in the Czech Republic and Poland suggest Budapest should make sure its stability takes root well before opening up.

Economists believe Hungary stands a good chance of avoiding a cycle of high growth followed by current account crises that have brought havoc to the Czech economy and now threatens Poland. Powerful elements of a formula that led to the plunge of the Czech crown in May -- a fast rise in consumer demand backed by spiralling wages and lack of efficiency gains -- are so far absent in Hungary.
"The forint will remain relatively strong and will remain well within its trading limit," said London-based HSBC analyst Nigel Rendell.
NO SHORT-TERM FOREIGN FUNDING NEEDED
Analysts point out that Hungary's current account and trade deficits are small, which means it does not require short-term foreign financing.
"The currency reserves are high and foreign direct capital is flowing in," said New York Broker analyst Zoltan Bereczki.
Hungary's international reserves totalled $8.4 billion in May when the current account deficit amounted to $446 million.

In a recent Reuters poll, the analysts' forecasts for the current account deficit averaged $2.19 billion for 1997 and $2.04 billion for 1998, compared with the government target of $2 billion for 1997 and $2 billion to $2.5 billion for 1998.
Foreign direct investment is expected to flow at up to $2 billion annually in the next two years, adding to some $14 billion invested so far.

The private sector is expected to account for about 70 percent of gross domestic product by the end of this year and a bold pension reform undertaken earlier this year is likely to improve fiscal balance. An additional source of foreign revenue, tourism, is expected to bring in about $1.3 billion annually.

The only major worry concerns wages, which grew seven percent in January-April in real terms, prompting the central bank to call on the government to make sure they rise no more than 2.5 percent next year.
CURRENCY OUTLOOK STABLE

"The fundamentals of the economy are so favourable that these will not create a speculation wave similar to what happened in the Czech Republic and Poland," said Gyorgy Szapary, vice president of the National Bank of Hungary (NBH).

Many analysts agree with Szapary that the forint is unlikely to drift much from the upper resistance level in the 4.5 percent wide intervention band, although some think it may come under some pressure next year.
"It will come down a little bit because as the economy picks up, the current account deficit will widen a little bit," Rendell said.
"We also think that due to the election in the early part of next year there will be a little bit of uncertainty in the market," he continued. "But this is not a dramatic thing."
Rendell forecast that the forint would go down to 209.00 to the dollar by the end of 1997 from the current 196.32, and to 222.00 by the end of 1998.

At the end of this year, the forint is likely to be one percent above the parity, still in the stronger half of the band, and by end-1998 it would go down to the centre of the intervention range, Rendell said.
Despite some uncertainties over the forint's position in the band and over the pace of decline in inflation, the forint will be a fairly predictable currency, analysts said.
Hungary plans to maintain its crawling peg devaluation system, and to cut the monthly rate in line with the fall in inflation and the increase in productivity.
The current 1.1 percent monthly depreciation rate will be cut to one percent on August 15 and analysts said it may go down to 0.7 to 0.8 percent by end-1998 depending on inflation.
Hungary hopes to cut inflation to some 18 percent in 1997 from 23.6 percent in 1996, and to 13.5 percent in 1998, while analyst forecasts average 18.46 and 14.63 percent respectively.

International organisations and analysts have told the government not to soften its fiscal policies before the 1998 elections and to agree a reasonable rise in real wages with employers and employees at talks due to close in the autumn.
The NBH and analysts agree that the widening of the forint intervention band could mean room for flexible monetary policy, but would also increase volatility to the forint.
CAUTIOUS LIBERALISATION
There are expectations at home and abroad for some currency liberalisation, yet the central bank says no major changes should be expected.

"We are still cautious," Judit Vadasz, head of the NBH regulatory department told Reuters, adding that press reports that the bank may allow foreigners to enter the currency futures markets were premature.
These restrictions are keeping forint trading turnover on Hungary's interbank foreign exchange market at low levels, at $150 to $250 million dollars a day, dealers and analysts said.

Under changes announced so far, foreign companies would be able to open branches in Hungary from next year and Hungarians would be allowed to buy shares in all companies and fund units registered in OECD countries. Apart from these measures, freeing capital flows, the NBH would also like to open the way for Hungarians to purchase real estate abroad.
But some argue that the opening of the currency market, either through wider bands or less restrictions on short-term flows, should come faster.
On Thursday, Hungarian foreign exchange dealers said they were losing business to London banks that are organising derivatives trading in the forint along with other East European currencies.
The volume of this off-shore trading is so far relatively small but it may increase as Hungary becomes a more attractive place to invest, they said.
